title: Sales Compensation Redesign
summary: Aligning sales incentives with gross profit, retention, price realization, strategic product mix, and durable growth.
definition: Sales Compensation Redesign is the process of changing quota, commission, bonus, and crediting rules so sales behavior matches the value creation plan.
whyItMatters: PE cares because sales teams often do exactly what they are paid to do, even when that destroys margin, retention, or pricing discipline.
commonProblems: Reps are paid on revenue regardless of gross margin or discounting.
Comp plans reward new bookings while ignoring churn, implementation quality, or cash collection.
Quota, territory, and crediting rules create conflict instead of focus.
diagnosticQuestions: What behavior does the current plan actually reward?
Where do commissions conflict with pricing, margin, retention, or strategic product goals?
Which plan changes will improve value without causing top-performer flight?
dataNeeded: Current compensation plans, quotas, accelerators, and crediting rules
Rep-level bookings, revenue, margin, churn, and discount data
Territory, segment, product, and customer profitability data
Sales attainment, turnover, and payout history
process: Diagnose current incentive behavior and economic leakage.
Define target behaviors tied to the VCP.
Model plan changes by rep, segment, product, and financial outcome.
Communicate changes with clear examples and transition rules.
Track behavior, attainment, payout, margin, and retention after rollout.
ebitdaLogic: Better sales compensation redirects rep behavior toward profitable growth, reduces discount leakage, improves retention quality, and makes revenue more valuable at exit.
caseExample: A sponsor-backed B2B services company shifts commissions from revenue-only to gross-profit-weighted bookings, reducing discount leakage while preserving top-rep motivation.
hundredDayPlan: Days 1-30: diagnose current plan economics and rep behavior.
Days 31-60: model new plan, test payout impacts, align leadership.
Days 61-100: communicate rollout, install dashboards, monitor behavior change.
commonMistakes: Changing compensation without modeling individual rep impact.
Overcomplicating the plan until no one understands what to sell.
Punishing top performers for legacy plan design without transition support.

articleSections.title: Translate Strategy into a Productivity Baseline
body: Begin with the value-creation plan, customer economics, and role design rather than last year's commission formula. Decide whether the company needs new logos, expansion, price realization, strategic-product adoption, faster collections, or retention, then identify which role can actually influence each outcome. Reconstruct two years of quotas, territories, bookings, gross margin, discounts, churn, ramp, payouts, and employment terms at the rep level. The CRO owns strategy and roles, finance owns affordability and accruals, HR and counsel own employment compliance, and RevOps owns source data and crediting logic.

Measure quota attainment distribution, time to productivity, voluntary attrition, payout as a percentage of revenue and gross profit, concentration of production, and performance by tenure, territory potential, and manager. A team with median attainment of 58%, only 8% of reps above quota, and frequent midyear quota relief probably has a capacity, territory, or goal-setting problem—not a motivation deficit. Conversely, 75% of reps above quota with rising discounts may indicate easy quotas or an overly rich rate. Separate plan defects from weak hiring, product-market fit, lead supply, enablement, and pricing.

Create design principles and non-negotiable gates before selecting mechanics. A plan should be explainable on one page, pay more for the outcomes the business values, preserve a meaningful upside path, avoid retroactive changes, and keep expected cost within the approved envelope. Establish target pay mix by role, quota methodology, target incentive, performance period, and risk tolerance. Do not place a metric in compensation merely because the board tracks it: the seller must control the result, data must be timely and auditable, and the company must be willing to adjudicate disputes consistently.
articleSections.callout: Compensation cannot repair an impossible quota, an empty territory, or a weak product; diagnose productivity before changing the payout curve.

articleSections.title: Design Quotas, Rates, Crediting, and Accelerators
body: Set quotas from addressable territory, historical production, pipeline creation, capacity, ramp, seasonality, and the operating plan. Reconcile aggregate quota capacity to the company target after expected vacancies and ramp, rather than adding an arbitrary cushion to every seller. Define whether attainment is based on bookings, annual contract value, revenue, gross profit, or cash and how cancellations, credits, foreign exchange, and multi-year terms behave. Assign quotas and territories before the period starts and document when management may make a prospective adjustment for a material territory or role change.

Build the rate from target incentive divided by quota, then shape accelerators around incremental economics. A rep with $120,000 target incentive and a $1.2 million quota has a 10% base rate. If payouts are 10% through 100% attainment, 15% from 100% to 125%, and 20% above 125%, calculate each band marginally rather than repricing all prior bookings. A rep at 120% on $1.44 million earns $120,000 on the first $1.2 million and $36,000 on the final $240,000, or $156,000 total. A threshold below which no payout is earned can still be added when partial performance creates no economic value.

Crediting rules need the same precision as rates. Define opportunity ownership, account transfers, sourced-versus-closed credit, team overlays, split approval, channel sales, renewals, expansions, product multipliers, discount penalties, clawbacks, and payment timing. Require an executed contract and clean CRM record before credit; align payout with invoicing or collections only where the rep influences those outcomes. Avoid uncapped windfalls on extraordinary house accounts by using predeclared large-deal treatment, not an after-the-fact cap. Every exception should cite the rule, approving authority, financial impact, and precedent classification.

articleSections.title: Model Scenarios and Prove Affordability
body: Model every incumbent rep and new-hire archetype at 0%, 50%, 80%, 100%, 120%, 150%, and 200% attainment using realistic deal timing, product mix, discounts, splits, cancellations, and ramp. Show cash payout, accounting expense, payout-to-revenue, payout-to-gross-profit, and contribution after delivery cost. The expected case should use an attainable distribution, not assume every rep lands exactly at quota. Stress a few large deals, delayed implementations, territory vacancies, and a strategic-product mix shift. Finance should reconcile modeled expense to the budget and determine monthly accrual mechanics before approval.

Test the worked rep economics against company returns. At 120% attainment, the example rep earns $156,000 of incentive on $1.44 million of bookings, an effective 10.8% rate. If bookings carry 70% gross margin, commission consumes 15.5% of gross profit before base salary, benefits, marketing, and implementation. If discounted deals carry only 50% margin, the same nominal rate consumes 21.7% of gross profit. A margin gate or lower credit on excessive discounting can protect economics, but it must use a price metric sellers understand and a preapproved exception for strategic deals.

Compare the new plan with the current plan and identify winners, losers, attrition risk, protected classes, and unintended incentives. Top performers should see credible upside, solid performers should not face a hidden pay cut at equal production, and low performers should not earn windfalls from territory luck. The compensation committee approves target cost and downside exposure; the board approves material pool changes; legal reviews wage-payment and notice requirements by jurisdiction. Reject a design if finance cannot calculate it from source transactions, managers cannot explain it, or scenarios reveal payout growth materially faster than profitable growth.

articleSections.title: Roll Out with Exception and Change Governance
body: Sequence rollout at least thirty days before the performance period where law and policy permit. Train managers first with a plan document, glossary, worked examples, territory and quota letter, payout calculator, frequently asked questions, and escalation path. Then deliver individual statements in live sessions and require acknowledgment. Use side-by-side examples to explain changes without promising any specific earnings outcome. For material transitions, consider a time-limited guarantee or draw tied to ramp or territory change, but model its cost and expiry; permanent protection weakens accountability and obscures whether quotas are achievable.

Create a compensation council with the CRO, CFO, HR, RevOps, and legal. It meets weekly through the first two payout cycles and monthly thereafter to approve disputes, exceptions, plan interpretations, and changes. Publish a decision log without sensitive individual details. Managers cannot promise special treatment, and payroll does not act on informal spreadsheets. Corrections should be prompt and documented, while prospective plan amendments require notice and scenario testing. Freeze mechanics during the period except for legal necessity or a material business change; frequent edits destroy trust and make behavioral attribution impossible.

Plan for resistance and failure. Reps may delay deals across periods, split opportunities strategically, over-discount to cross a threshold, sell low-fit products, hoard accounts, or contest CRM ownership. Instrument these behaviors before launch and use audit rules rather than rumor. If payout errors occur, disclose the cause, correction, and control improvement. If top sellers threaten departure, evaluate their economic and cultural contribution without creating secret guarantees that invalidate the plan. Change management succeeds when sellers can predict pay from approved transactions and believe identical facts receive identical treatment.

articleSections.title: Monitor Behavior, Recalibrate, and Build Exit Proof
body: Run a monthly behavior dashboard that links attainment and payout to price realization, gross margin, product mix, win rate, sales cycle, churn, collections, and customer concentration. Analyze distributions by role, manager, tenure, and territory potential. Finance reconciles calculated payout to payroll and the ledger; RevOps audits transaction credit; HR monitors retention and disputes; the CRO reviews commercial effects. Use leading indicators after one month but wait for enough selling cycles before redesigning. A dip in bookings may reflect seasonality or product issues, while a sharp discount shift immediately after launch is stronger plan evidence.

Validate benefits relative to the frozen pre-plan cohort. If average discount improves from 14% to 10% on $30 million of comparable gross bookings, the gross revenue benefit is about $1.2 million before volume, churn, and mix effects. Subtract incremental commission, lost volume, implementation cost, and credits, then confirm realized invoice price and cash collection. Do not claim strategic-product growth if the product was reclassified or bundled, and do not attribute retention improvement entirely to sellers. The benefit ledger should name the causal mechanism, counterfactual, evidence, owner, and finance approval.

Recalibrate annually, or sooner only when a defined trigger occurs: territory potential shifts materially, attainment distribution falls outside the approved band, payout cost breaches its envelope, margin or retention deteriorates, or a new product changes economics. Exit proof includes signed plans, quota methodology, scenario model, attainment and payout history, exception log, payroll reconciliation, behavior trends, and validated economics. Buyers should see a controlled incentive system that produces profitable growth without dependence on discretionary deals. Unexplained overrides, retroactive changes, or commission liabilities will instead become diligence and retention risks.
